questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes 'interpretation' from 'construction' as those terms are used in this chapter?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — interpretation distinguished from construction

options.text: Interpretation is done by the legislature and construction by the courts
options.explanation: Both are done by courts. The legislature/court divide belongs to the classification of interpretation into authentic and usual legal interpretation, not to the interpretation-construction distinction.

options.text: Interpretation ascertains the meaning the legislature expressed in the words used; construction draws conclusions about situations the words do not address in terms
options.explanation: Correct. Interpretation looks at the words; construction applies them to a case the language leaves open. Courts and textbooks use the words interchangeably, but this is the distinction they draw when they draw one.

options.text: Interpretation applies only to ambiguous provisions; construction applies only to clear ones
options.explanation: Reversed and wrong. A clear provision still has to be interpreted; construction is precisely what is needed when the words run out.

options.text: Interpretation is binding on lower courts while construction is merely persuasive
options.explanation: No such hierarchy exists. Whether a reading binds depends on the court that gave it, not on the label attached to the process.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the reasons a statute may require interpretation?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — causes of uncertainty in statutory language

options.text: A word used in the statute bears two natural meanings
options.explanation: Ambiguity is a classic cause. 'Charge', 'issue' and 'sanction' each carry more than one ordinary sense.

options.text: The legislature did not foresee the situation that has arisen
options.explanation: Incomplete drafting is a recognised cause: statutes are written before the disputes they govern exist.

options.text: Two provisions of the same Act, read literally, pull in opposite directions
options.explanation: Internal conflict is a recognised cause, and it is what harmonious construction exists to resolve.

options.text: The court considers the policy adopted by the legislature to be unwise
options.explanation: Correct. This is NOT a ground. The court's task is to find what the legislature said, never to substitute its own view of good policy; an unwise but clear provision is simply applied.

questions.stem: An interpretation clause inserted by the legislature into the Act itself is an example of:
questions.sourceRef: Classification of interpretation — legal (authentic and usual) and doctrinal

options.text: Authentic legal interpretation
options.explanation: Correct. Legal (authoritative) interpretation is either authentic — given by the legislature itself, through an interpretation clause, an Explanation or a declaratory Act — or usual, given by the courts. An interpretation clause is the standard example of the authentic kind.

options.text: Usual legal interpretation
options.explanation: Usual legal interpretation is what a court does when it decides a case. The legislature is not a court.

options.text: Doctrinal grammatical interpretation
options.explanation: Doctrinal interpretation is the work of jurists and commentators and is persuasive only. A statutory definition binds.

options.text: Doctrinal logical interpretation
options.explanation: Same error. Nothing the legislature enacts is 'doctrinal'; doctrinal interpretation is extra-judicial commentary.

questions.stem: What is the correct relationship between grammatical and logical construction?
questions.sourceRef: Classification of interpretation — grammatical and logical construction

options.text: The court may adopt either approach as it thinks fit in any case
options.explanation: Wrong sequencing. Logical construction is a fallback, not a free choice, and an answer in these terms loses the sequencing mark.

options.text: Logical construction always governs, because the intention of the legislature matters more than its words
options.explanation: The words are the primary evidence of the intention. Starting with intention and working back to the words inverts the exercise.

options.text: Grammatical construction governs; logical construction is reached only where the grammatical result is ambiguous, absurd, repugnant or defeats the object of the Act
options.explanation: Correct. The court begins with the words on the page and moves beyond them only on one of those four triggers — and then departs only so far as is necessary.

options.text: Grammatical construction applies to old statutes and logical construction to modern ones
options.explanation: There is no such division. Age of the statute matters to contemporanea expositio, not to this classification.

questions.stem: Under the literal or grammatical rule, where the words of a statute are plain and unambiguous, the court must:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — literal or grammatical rule

readLink.label: Read: The literal or grammatical rule →

options.text: Give them their ordinary meaning only if the result is fair to both parties
options.explanation: Fairness is not the test. The literal rule is indifferent to whether the outcome is congenial; only absurdity or repugnancy disturbs it.

options.text: Prefer the meaning that best carries out the policy the court believes Parliament had in mind
options.explanation: That is logical or purposive construction, and it is not available while the words remain plain.

options.text: Give them their ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning, whatever the consequence
options.explanation: Correct. The letter of the law is taken as the best evidence of its intention; the court neither adds words nor subtracts them, and hardship is no ground for departing.

options.text: Refer to the Statement of Objects and Reasons before applying them
options.explanation: External aids are admissible only where the language is ambiguous. Plain words do not open the door to them.

questions.stem: A statute prohibits bringing 'any dog' into the reading room of a public library. A visitor brings a goat. Applying the literal rule, the correct position is:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — casus omissus

readLink.label: Read: The literal or grammatical rule →

options.text: The goat is not prohibited; the omission is a casus omissus which the court will not supply
options.explanation: Correct. 'Dog' is plain, undefined and carries no technical sense here. A case the legislature has failed to provide for cannot be supplied by the court; the remedy is an amendment substituting 'any animal'.

options.text: The goat is prohibited, because the golden rule permits the court to avoid the absurd result of admitting a goat but not a dog
options.explanation: The result is unsatisfactory, not absurd. The section works perfectly well as far as it goes, and the golden rule needs absurdity or repugnancy, not mere incompleteness.

options.text: The goat is prohibited, because the mischief the Act addresses is animals in libraries
options.explanation: The mischief rule chooses between readings the words can bear. 'Dog' cannot bear the meaning 'goat', so there is nothing for the rule to choose between.

options.text: The court must refer the question to the legislature before deciding
options.explanation: Courts decide the case before them; they do not refer questions of construction back to the legislature. They simply apply the words as they stand.

questions.stem: Which statement about the meaning given to words under the literal rule is INCORRECT?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ordinary popular sense and technical sense

readLink.label: Read: The literal or grammatical rule →

options.text: Words are ordinarily read in their popular sense
options.explanation: This is a true statement of the rule: the ordinary popular sense is the default reading.

options.text: Words used in relation to a particular trade, science or art bear their technical sense
options.explanation: Also true. Where the statute deals with a specialised field, the specialised meaning is the natural one.

options.text: A word defined by the Act bears the defined meaning throughout, unless the context otherwise requires
options.explanation: Also true. That is the effect of a definition clause, subject to its standard escape.

options.text: Where the same word appears twice in a statute, the court presumes the legislature intended different meanings on each occasion
options.explanation: Correct. This is the incorrect statement, and so the answer. The presumption runs the other way: the same word is presumed to bear the SAME meaning throughout, and different words are presumed to mean different things.

questions.stem: The golden rule permits a court to depart from the ordinary grammatical meaning of the words where that meaning leads to:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — golden rule

options.text: Hardship or inconvenience to one of the parties
options.explanation: Hardship is not enough. A tax that falls heavily, or a limitation period that bars a genuine claim, is hard but not absurd.

options.text: Some absurdity, repugnance or inconsistency with the rest of the instrument
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the three triggers, and the threshold is deliberately high — the result must be absurd or repugnant, not merely unfortunate.

options.text: A result the court considers contrary to the public interest
options.explanation: The court's own view of the public interest is not a ground for departing from clear words; that would be legislating.

options.text: Any ambiguity in the language of the section
options.explanation: Ambiguity is the trigger for the mischief rule, not the golden rule. The golden rule operates where the literal meaning is clear but the result it produces is absurd or repugnant.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Golden rule — extent of departure
questions.stem: Once the golden rule is engaged, how far may the court modify the ordinary meaning of the words?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — golden rule, extent of modification

options.text: Only so far as is necessary to avoid the absurdity or inconsistency, and no further
options.explanation: Correct. This is the limit that carries the marks. The court removes the absurdity and then stops; it does not go on to rewrite the provision into what it thinks the ideal rule would be.

options.text: As far as is needed to give the provision the meaning the court believes the legislature would have chosen had it considered the point
options.explanation: That is rewriting on a hypothesis about legislative preference and goes far beyond the rule.

options.text: The court may substitute an entirely new provision, provided it records reasons
options.explanation: No court may substitute a provision. Even under the golden rule the reading must be one the words can bear.

options.text: There is no limit, since the absurdity shows the words were not intended to be applied literally
options.explanation: Absurdity in one application does not discard the words altogether; it licenses the minimum modification that removes the absurdity.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Heydon's case — the four questions
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four matters a court considers under the mischief rule in Heydon's case?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — mischief rule, Heydon's case

readLink.label: Read: The mischief rule in Heydon's case →

options.text: What was the law before the making of the Act
options.explanation: This is the first question — the prior legal position the Act replaced.

options.text: What was the mischief and defect for which the prior law did not provide
options.explanation: This is the second question — the gap or abuse that provoked the Act.

options.text: What penalty the legislature has prescribed for contravention of the Act
options.explanation: Correct. This is not one of the four. They are: the prior law; the mischief and defect; the remedy the legislature has resolved and appointed; and the true reason of the remedy. The quantum of punishment forms no part of the inquiry.

options.text: What is the true reason of the remedy
options.explanation: This is the fourth question — why the legislature chose the machinery it did.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Mischief rule — the court's duty
questions.stem: Having answered the four questions in Heydon's case, the court's duty is to adopt the construction that will:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — suppress the mischief, advance the remedy

readLink.label: Read: The mischief rule in Heydon's case →

options.text: Advance the mischief and suppress the remedy
options.explanation: Inverted. The rule exists to defeat the evil, not to protect it.

options.text: Suppress the mischief and advance the remedy, and defeat subtle inventions and evasions that would continue the mischief
options.explanation: Correct. That is the classic formulation, and the reference to subtle inventions and evasions is what makes the rule so useful against devices designed to sidestep a remedial statute.

options.text: Give the narrowest possible meaning to the remedial provision so as to limit interference with existing rights
options.explanation: Narrow construction of a remedial provision is the opposite of what the rule directs. Strict construction belongs to penal and taxing statutes.

options.text: Prefer the reading that imposes the lightest burden on the person sought to be made liable
options.explanation: That is the penal-statute canon (ambiguity favours the accused), not the mischief rule.

questions.stem: Which statement about the limits of the mischief rule is CORRECT?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — limits of the mischief rule

readLink.label: Read: The mischief rule in Heydon's case →

options.text: Once the mischief is identified, the court may insert the words needed to suppress it
options.explanation: The rule never licenses inserting words. It tells the court which of the available readings to prefer.

options.text: The rule applies with equal force to penal and taxing statutes
options.explanation: It does not. In penal and taxing statutes strict construction governs, and a mischief-based extension of liability is not permitted.

options.text: The mischief may be identified from the judge's own assessment of what society needs
options.explanation: The mischief must come from legitimate sources — the prior law, the preamble, the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the historical setting — not from judicial policy preference.

options.text: The rule operates only where the words are ambiguous or capable of two readings; it cannot overturn a clear one
options.explanation: Correct. The mischief tells the court which possible reading to prefer. Where only one reading is possible, no amount of mischief reasoning displaces it.

questions.stem: Where two provisions of the same statute appear to conflict, the rule of harmonious construction requires the court to:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — harmonious construction

options.text: So construe them that effect is given to both, so that neither is reduced to a dead letter
options.explanation: Correct. The statute is read as a whole and the provisions are reconciled if reconciliation is at all possible — usually by confining each to its own field.

options.text: Prefer the provision appearing earlier in the Act, as it states the general scheme
options.explanation: Order of appearance decides nothing. A later special provision commonly qualifies an earlier general one.

options.text: Declare the later of the two provisions void for repugnancy
options.explanation: A court does not strike down one provision of an Act for conflicting with another; it reconciles them.

options.text: Refer the conflict to the rule of ejusdem generis
options.explanation: Ejusdem generis addresses general words following specific words in a list. It has nothing to do with reconciling two conflicting provisions.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Harmonious construction — failure and fallback
questions.stem: Sections 20 and 44 of an Act cannot both operate on the same facts. Section 44 deals specifically with the class of case in dispute; section 20 is general. What follows?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — harmonious construction, order of resolution

options.text: Section 20 prevails, because a general provision states the legislative policy for the whole Act
options.explanation: A general provision does not swallow a special one. That would leave section 44 with nothing to operate on.

options.text: Both provisions must be applied cumulatively, and the stricter requirement observed
options.explanation: Cumulative application is not the technique. Harmonious construction confines each provision to its own field; it does not stack them.

options.text: Section 44 governs the facts it specifically addresses, and section 20 governs the rest — generalia specialibus non derogant
options.explanation: Correct. Reconciliation is attempted first; where the two cannot both operate on the same facts, the special provision governs those facts and the general provision continues to govern everything else.

options.text: The court must ignore section 44, since harmony is achieved by applying a single rule
options.explanation: Achieving 'harmony' by ignoring one provision is exactly the subtraction the rule forbids. Harmonious construction is reconciliation, not deletion.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Purposive construction and the mischief rule
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between purposive construction and the mischief rule?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — purposive construction

options.text: They are unrelated: the mischief rule looks at the words while purposive construction looks at the preamble
options.explanation: Both look beyond the words. The mischief rule is not a form of literal construction.

options.text: Purposive construction is the wider, modern successor of the mischief rule: it looks to the positive object of the Act rather than only to the defect the Act cured, and needs no earlier law to work on
options.explanation: Correct. Every mischief-rule case is a purposive case, but not every purposive case involves a mischief — purposive construction works even on a wholly new subject with no predecessor legislation.

options.text: Purposive construction is narrower than the mischief rule, because it is confined to remedial statutes
options.explanation: It is wider, not narrower, and it is not confined to remedial statutes.

options.text: Purposive construction permits a court to give words a meaning they cannot bear, provided the purpose is clear
options.explanation: This is the one thing purposive construction may never do. It selects among meanings the words can bear; purpose does not displace clear language.

questions.stem: A welfare enactment uses a word capable of two meanings; one meaning would allow employers to sidestep the protection entirely by a simple change of paperwork. Which rule is the court most likely to apply, and why?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — sequence of application

readLink.label: Read: The primary rules side by side →

options.text: The literal rule, because the word has an ordinary meaning that can be applied
options.explanation: The literal rule cannot decide the case: the word bears two meanings, so 'the ordinary meaning' does not identify one of them.

options.text: The golden rule, because one reading is inconvenient for the workers
options.explanation: Inconvenience is not the golden-rule trigger, and the golden rule operates on a single clear meaning that produces an absurdity — not on a genuine two-way ambiguity.

options.text: Harmonious construction, because two readings of the same word conflict
options.explanation: Harmonious construction reconciles two conflicting PROVISIONS, not two possible meanings of one word.

options.text: The mischief rule, because the words are ambiguous, the Act is remedial, and the reading that permits evasion would leave the mischief in place
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions for Heydon's rule are present, and the rule expressly directs courts to defeat subtle inventions and evasions designed to continue the mischief.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a condition for the application of the rule of ejusdem generis?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ejusdem generis, conditions of application

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

options.text: The general words must be capable of being given a meaning that benefits the person affected
options.explanation: Correct. This is not a condition. Ejusdem generis is a neutral rule of language; whom the restriction happens to help is irrelevant to whether it applies.

options.text: The statute must contain an enumeration of specific words
options.explanation: This is a condition. Without a list of specific words there is nothing from which a genus can be drawn.

options.text: The subjects of the enumeration must constitute a genus or category
options.explanation: This is the central condition, and the one most often forgotten.

options.text: The genus must not be exhausted by the enumeration, and the general words must follow the specific words
options.explanation: Both are conditions. If the genus is exhausted the general words would be redundant, and general words that PRECEDE an enumeration are not cut down by it.

questions.stem: A section refers to 'books, pamphlets, houses, motor cars and other things'. How should 'other things' be construed?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ejusdem generis, absence of a genus

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

options.text: Confined to printed material, since books and pamphlets appear first in the list
options.explanation: Position in the list does not create a genus. Houses and motor cars are in the same enumeration and are not printed material.

options.text: Confined to movable property, since three of the four specific items are movable
options.explanation: A genus must cover the enumeration, not a majority of it. 'Houses' defeats any movable-property category.

options.text: At its natural width, because the specific words do not constitute a genus and ejusdem generis therefore has no application
options.explanation: Correct. Books, pamphlets, houses and motor cars share no common characteristic beyond being listed together, so there is no genus to confine the general words, and they carry their full meaning.

options.text: The section is void for uncertainty
options.explanation: Courts do not strike down provisions for this kind of drafting looseness. They construe the general words at their natural width.

questions.stem: A levy applies to 'vegetables, fruits, flowers and all other perishable articles whatsoever'. What is the effect of the word 'whatsoever'?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ejusdem generis, contrary legislative intention

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

options.text: None; ejusdem generis applies regardless of the drafting, because a genus is present
options.explanation: The presence of a genus is only one of the conditions. A manifest contrary intention defeats the rule even where a genus exists.

options.text: It shows a contrary legislative intention, so the general words are not confined to the horticultural genus and are read at full width
options.explanation: Correct. 'Whatsoever' — like 'whether or not of the same kind as the foregoing' — is a standard drafting signal that the legislature meant the general words to be unrestricted, and it displaces ejusdem generis.

options.text: It converts the provision into an exhaustive list, so only the three named items are covered
options.explanation: 'Whatsoever' widens the general words; it does not delete them and leave only the specific items.

options.text: It makes the provision penal, so it must be strictly construed
options.explanation: A levy is a taxing provision, not a penal one, and 'whatsoever' says nothing about the character of the statute.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Ejusdem generis — general words first
questions.stem: A clause reads: 'any vehicle, including a car, truck or bus'. A dispute arises whether a tractor is covered. Which analysis is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ejusdem generis, order of the words

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

options.text: The tractor is excluded, because ejusdem generis confines 'vehicle' to the three named types
options.explanation: Ejusdem generis operates on general words that FOLLOW specific words. Here the general word comes first.

options.text: The tractor is excluded, because 'including' makes the list exhaustive
options.explanation: 'Includes' is an extensive formula: it preserves the ordinary meaning of the word and adds to it. It does not make a list exhaustive.

options.text: The tractor is excluded, because a genus of road passenger and goods carriers is present
options.explanation: Even if such a genus could be described, it is irrelevant — the structural condition for the maxim is missing.

options.text: The tractor is covered: the general word precedes the enumeration, so it is not cut down by it, and 'including' is extensive rather than exhaustive
options.explanation: Correct. Two independent reasons point the same way — the general word is not preceded by the specific words, and the inclusive formula widens rather than confines.

questions.stem: The maxim noscitur a sociis means that:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — noscitur a sociis

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

options.text: A doubtful word takes its meaning from the words associated with it
options.explanation: Correct. Literally, a word is known by the company it keeps. Words grouped together in a statute are presumed to be used in a related sense and to take colour from one another.

options.text: General words following specific words are confined to the genus of the specific words
options.explanation: That is ejusdem generis, which is a specialised application of noscitur a sociis, not the maxim itself.

options.text: The express mention of one thing excludes another
options.explanation: That is expressio unius est exclusio alterius.

options.text: A construction that makes the provision workable is preferred to one that makes it useless
options.explanation: That is ut res magis valeat quam pereat.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis distinguished
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes noscitur a sociis from ejusdem generis?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — relationship between the two maxims

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

options.text: They are two names for the same rule, used interchangeably by courts
options.explanation: They are related but not identical; one is the parent, the other the specialised application.

options.text: Noscitur a sociis applies to any string of associated words and needs no general-words-after-specific-words structure; ejusdem generis is its narrower application, which does
options.explanation: Correct. Ejusdem generis is a species of noscitur a sociis, with the extra structural requirement that general words follow an enumeration constituting a genus.

options.text: Noscitur a sociis applies only to penal statutes and ejusdem generis only to taxing statutes
options.explanation: Neither maxim is confined to a class of statute. Both are general rules of language.

options.text: Ejusdem generis is the wider rule and noscitur a sociis is the narrower application of it
options.explanation: Reversed. Noscitur a sociis is the wider rule.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
questions.stem: Which statement about expressio unius est exclusio alterius is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — expressio unius est exclusio alterius and its limits

readLink.label: Read: Other subsidiary rules of construction →

options.text: It is an inflexible rule of law: whatever is not expressly mentioned is always excluded
options.explanation: It is a maxim of inference, not a rule of law, and it is defeated in several standard situations.

options.text: It applies only to Schedules and Forms, not to sections
options.explanation: There is no such confinement. It applies wherever a statute enumerates.

options.text: It is a maxim of inference: express mention of one thing suggests the exclusion of another, but it fails where the enumeration is illustrative, where the omission is an oversight, or where the mention was made ex abundanti cautela
options.explanation: Correct. All three qualifications matter — words such as 'such as' or 'including' show an illustrative list, and a mention made out of abundant caution carries no negative implication.

options.text: It requires the presence of a genus among the enumerated items
options.explanation: A genus is a condition of ejusdem generis, not of expressio unius.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Ut res magis valeat quam pereat
questions.stem: Two readings of a section are possible. One makes part of the section redundant; the other gives every word work to do. Which maxim decides, and how?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ut res magis valeat quam pereat

readLink.label: Read: Other subsidiary rules of construction →

options.text: Ut res magis valeat quam pereat — the reading that makes the provision effective and workable is preferred, and surplusage is not to be presumed
options.explanation: Correct. The maxim means 'let the thing have effect rather than perish'. Courts lean against constructions that render a provision unworkable, nugatory or redundant, since every word is presumed to have been used for a purpose.

options.text: Contemporanea expositio — the reading adopted by the department when the Act was passed is preferred
options.explanation: Contemporaneous exposition is about official understanding at the time of enactment, not about avoiding redundancy, and it is weak for modern statutes.

options.text: Reddendo singula singulis — each word is referred to its own subject
options.explanation: Reddendo singula singulis distributes subjects and objects in a compound sentence. It does not resolve redundancy.

options.text: Generalia specialibus non derogant — the more specific reading prevails
options.explanation: That maxim resolves a conflict between a general and a special provision, not a choice between an effective and a redundant reading.

questions.stem: A later general Act limits every licence suspension to three months. An earlier special Act allows suspension of a market trader's licence for up to six months. In the absence of any express repeal, what is the position?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — generalia specialibus non derogant

readLink.label: Read: Other subsidiary rules of construction →

options.text: The later Act repeals the earlier one entirely, since the legislature is presumed to know the existing law
options.explanation: Knowledge of the existing law supports the OPPOSITE inference — that the legislature did not intend to disturb a special provision without saying so.

options.text: The two provisions are irreconcilable, so the earlier Act is void
options.explanation: One statute does not become void for conflicting with another. The court reconciles them.

options.text: The six-month period survives only if the earlier Act contains a saving clause
options.explanation: No saving clause is needed. The presumption against implied repeal of a special Act does the work.

options.text: The special six-month provision continues to govern market traders' licences: a later general Act is not presumed to repeal an earlier special Act by implication
options.explanation: Correct. Generalia specialibus non derogant works between statutes as well as within one, and it is reinforced by the presumption against implied repeal. Only a clear intention to displace the special provision would change the answer.

questions.stem: Which statement about the maxim contemporanea expositio est optima et fortissima in lege is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — contemporanea expositio

readLink.label: Read: Other subsidiary rules of construction →

options.text: It permits the meaning of a modern statute to be settled conclusively by the administering department's circular
options.explanation: Departmental circulars never bind a court, and the maxim has little or no application to a modern statute the court can read for itself.

options.text: The meaning given to a statute by those who administered it at or near the time of its enactment, and the usage that followed, is strong evidence of its meaning — but it applies mainly to old statutes and always yields to clear words
options.explanation: Correct. All three elements matter: contemporaneous official understanding, long usage, and the two limits — old statutes, and no application against clear language.

options.text: It requires a court to prefer the construction that was most favourable to the subject at the time of enactment
options.explanation: That confuses the maxim with the strict-construction canon for taxing and penal statutes.

options.text: It permits a later statute to change the meaning the earlier one bore from the date of its enactment
options.explanation: That is a question about declaratory and amending Acts as external aids, not about contemporaneous exposition.

questions.stem: A clause reads: 'The Registrar or the Tribunal may, on an application or of its own motion, cancel the registration or wind up the company.' Applying reddendo singula singulis, the correct reading is:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — reddendo singula singulis

readLink.label: Read: Other subsidiary rules of construction →

options.text: Both authorities may exercise both powers by both routes, since the word 'or' is disjunctive throughout
options.explanation: Reading every phrase as applying to everything is precisely what the maxim prevents, and here it produces the absurdity of a Registrar winding up a company.

options.text: The clause is void for uncertainty and must be redrafted
options.explanation: Courts construe clauses of this kind; they do not strike them down for compound drafting.

options.text: Each authority is matched with the power that properly belongs to it — the Registrar cancelling the registration and the Tribunal winding up the company — and each with its appropriate route
options.explanation: Correct. Reddendo singula singulis means rendering each to each: where a sentence contains several subjects and several objects, each is referred to its appropriate counterpart rather than every phrase being applied to everything.

options.text: Only the first-named authority and the first-named power are operative
options.explanation: The maxim distributes the phrases; it does not delete all but the first of them.

questions.stem: Which statement about the presumption of constitutionality is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Presumptions in interpretation — constitutionality and reading down

options.text: A statute is presumed valid; the burden lies on the person challenging it, and where two readings are possible the one that keeps the Act constitutional is preferred
options.explanation: Correct. The last limb is the technique known as reading down, and it follows from the presumption together with ut res magis valeat quam pereat.

options.text: A statute is presumed invalid until the State demonstrates its competence
options.explanation: The burden runs the other way. The challenger must establish invalidity.

options.text: The presumption is irrebuttable once the Act has received assent
options.explanation: No presumption in this chapter is irrebuttable. A statute clearly unconstitutional on every possible reading is struck down.

options.text: The presumption applies only to taxing statutes
options.explanation: It applies to statutes generally.

questions.stem: An amendment changes the forum before which an appeal must be filed. Existing appeals are pending. Which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Presumptions in interpretation — presumption against retrospective operation

options.text: The amendment cannot apply at all to pending appeals, because every statute is presumed prospective
options.explanation: The presumption against retrospectivity attaches to SUBSTANTIVE provisions. A change of forum is procedural.

options.text: The amendment applies to all matters, including proceedings already finally decided, because procedure is always retrospective
options.explanation: Even a procedural amendment does not reopen proceedings already concluded, and 'always' overstates the presumption.

options.text: The amendment applies only if it says so expressly
options.explanation: Express words are needed for a substantive provision to operate retrospectively, not for a procedural one.

options.text: The amendment is presumed to apply to pending appeals, because a purely procedural provision is presumed retrospective — no one has a vested right in a procedure — subject to the qualification that a change destroying an accrued right is not treated as merely procedural
options.explanation: Correct. The substantive/procedural divide is the examined point, and the qualification about accrued rights is what turns a good answer into a full-marks one.

questions.stem: A section creating an offence is silent as to the mental element required. What does the court presume?
questions.sourceRef: Presumptions in interpretation — mens rea in penal statutes

options.text: That the offence is one of strict liability, since the legislature said nothing about intention
options.explanation: The silence works the other way: the presumption is in favour of mens rea, and strict liability must be shown.

options.text: That mens rea — a guilty mind — is required, the presumption being rebuttable by express exclusion or by the clear implication of a regulatory or welfare statute
options.explanation: Correct. The presumption is a strong one in penal statutes, and it is displaced only by express words or by the necessary implication of the statutory scheme.

options.text: That the burden of proving innocence lies on the accused
options.explanation: Presumptions of construction do not shift the burden of proof in a criminal trial.

options.text: That the section is void for vagueness
options.explanation: Silence as to the mental element is not vagueness; it is filled by the presumption.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Strict construction of penal statutes
questions.stem: Which statement about the strict construction of a penal statute is INCORRECT?
questions.sourceRef: Strict construction — penal statutes

options.text: An act is not an offence unless it falls clearly within the words of the section
options.explanation: This is a true statement of the canon.

options.text: Where the section is genuinely ambiguous, the construction favourable to the accused is adopted
options.explanation: Also true, and the best-known consequence of strict construction.

options.text: Because the penalty is severe, the court must read the section narrowly even where the words plainly cover the accused's conduct
options.explanation: Correct. This is the incorrect statement, and so the answer. Strict construction does not license a perverse or unnatural reading: where the words plainly cover the conduct, the accused is convicted, and the severity of the penalty is no reason to narrow clear words.

options.text: The definition of an offence is not extended by analogy or by considerations of policy
options.explanation: True. Extension by analogy is exactly what strict construction forbids.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly states how the different parts of a taxing statute are construed?
questions.sourceRef: Strict construction — taxing statutes, charging and machinery provisions

options.text: Charging provision — strict; exemption — strict, with the burden on the assessee; machinery or procedural provision — liberal, so as to make the charge workable
options.explanation: Correct. All three limbs are examined. The governing idea is that there is no equity about a tax and nothing is to be read in or implied into the charge, while the machinery must be construed so that the charge can actually be collected.

options.text: Charging provision — liberal; exemption — liberal; machinery — strict
options.explanation: Every limb is inverted. A liberal charging provision would tax a person the words do not catch.

options.text: Charging provision — strict; exemption — liberal, with the burden on the revenue; machinery — strict
options.explanation: An exemption is construed strictly and the assessee must show that he falls within it; and strict construction of the machinery would frustrate collection.

options.text: All provisions of a taxing statute are construed strictly without distinction
options.explanation: This ignores the machinery exception, which is a standard examination point.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Beneficial legislation and its limits
questions.stem: Which statement about the liberal construction of beneficial or welfare legislation is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Liberal construction — beneficial and welfare legislation

options.text: Every provision of a welfare Act, including its penal provisions, is construed liberally in favour of the protected class
options.explanation: A penal provision inside a welfare Act is still construed strictly. A person is not punished by a generous reading.

options.text: Liberal construction permits the court to relax an eligibility condition the legislature laid down, if the claimant deserves the benefit
options.explanation: Liberal construction operates only where the provision is capable of two constructions. It cannot rewrite an eligibility condition.

options.text: Beneficial legislation is always given retrospective effect
options.explanation: The correct statement is far narrower: where a beneficial or curative provision is capable of two readings, the court MAY give it retrospective effect to advance the benefit.

options.text: Where a provision of a welfare Act is capable of two constructions, the one more favourable to the class the Act protects is adopted, so that the benefit is not defeated by a narrow reading
options.explanation: Correct. The condition — capable of two constructions — is what makes the statement accurate, and it is where most scripts lose the mark.

questions.stem: A section provides that the Assessor 'shall' complete the assessment list by 30 June. He completes it on 12 July. Which approach does a court take?
questions.sourceRef: Mandatory and directory provisions — the auxiliary verb is not conclusive

options.text: The list is void, because 'shall' is always mandatory
options.explanation: 'Shall' is a strong indicator but is not conclusive; draftsmen use it loosely, and the courts decide by the object and scheme of the statute.

options.text: The court examines the object of the provision, whether the statute states a consequence for breach, whether anyone is prejudiced and whether treating it as mandatory would cause serious general inconvenience — and here would likely hold it directory, so the list stands
options.explanation: Correct. A time limit cast on a public officer for the orderly conduct of administration, over which the affected persons have no control, is the classic directory provision; holding every late list void would cause serious general inconvenience.

options.text: The list is valid because 'shall' in a revenue statute always means 'may'
options.explanation: No such rule exists. The result is reached by applying the tests, not by a blanket equivalence.

options.text: The court must strike down section 8 as unworkable
options.explanation: Courts do not invalidate a provision because an officer missed its deadline.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Consequence of non-compliance as a test
questions.stem: Which pairing of indicator and conclusion is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Mandatory and directory provisions — stated consequence, negative language

options.text: The statute declares the act void on breach → mandatory; the statute prescribes only a penalty on the defaulting officer → usually directory
options.explanation: Correct. Where the legislature declares the act void it has said that non-compliance destroys validity. Where it prescribes only a penalty it has supplied its own consequence, which usually indicates it did not intend invalidity in addition.

options.text: The statute prescribes a penalty on breach → mandatory; the statute declares the act void → directory
options.explanation: Both limbs are inverted.

options.text: The provision is expressed in negative or prohibitory form ('no order shall be made unless') → directory
options.explanation: Negative or prohibitory language is one of the strongest indicators that a provision is MANDATORY.

options.text: The provision confers a safeguard on an identified individual, such as notice and hearing → directory
options.explanation: A right or safeguard conferred on an individual is usually mandatory, precisely because its breach prejudices that person.

questions.stem: Which statement about the weight of internal aids is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Internal aids — preamble, headings, marginal notes, short title

options.text: A marginal note is part of the Act and may control the plain meaning of the section beside it
options.explanation: The marginal note is the weakest internal aid: it is generally not part of the Act and is not inserted by the legislature. Marginal notes in the Constitution are the recognised exception.

options.text: The short title is a legitimate guide to the general scope and object of the Act
options.explanation: The short title serves identification only. It is the LONG title that indicates scope and object.

options.text: The preamble is part of the Act and is a key to its object and policy, but it cannot be used against plain words
options.explanation: Correct. The preamble may be used to resolve ambiguity and to identify the policy of the Act; like every aid, it yields to unambiguous language.

options.text: A heading prefixed to a group of sections overrides the sections it governs
options.explanation: A heading may be referred to where a section is ambiguous, but it cannot control the plain meaning of the section.

questions.stem: A definition clause provides: "'infrastructure facility' includes a road, a bridge and a port." What is the effect?
questions.sourceRef: Internal aids — definition clauses, restrictive and extensive formulae

options.text: The expression is confined to roads, bridges and ports, the list being exhaustive
options.explanation: That would be the effect of 'means', or of 'means and includes'. 'Includes' does not close the list.

options.text: The expression keeps its ordinary meaning and is extended to cover the three items listed, the enumeration being illustrative and not exhaustive
options.explanation: Correct. 'Includes' is the extensive or inclusive formula: the word retains its ordinary meaning and gets more. Contrast 'means' (restrictive and exhaustive) and 'means and includes' (exhaustive despite the word 'includes').

options.text: The three items are excluded from the ordinary meaning of the expression
options.explanation: An inclusive definition adds; it never subtracts.

options.text: The clause is a legal fiction and must be carried to its logical conclusion
options.explanation: 'Is deemed to be' creates a legal fiction, and even then only for the purpose stated. 'Includes' is simply an extensive definition.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · External aids and their limits
questions.stem: Which statement about external aids is correct?
questions.sourceRef: External aids — Statement of Objects and Reasons, parliamentary debates, dictionaries

options.text: The Statement of Objects and Reasons accompanying a Bill is conclusive as to the meaning of the enacted section
options.explanation: It is admissible to understand the background, the mischief and the purpose — but not to construe the section, because the Bill may have been amended during its passage.

options.text: A dictionary meaning prevails over a definition contained in the Act
options.explanation: A statutory definition always prevails. A dictionary gives all possible meanings; the court must pick the one that fits the context.

options.text: A foreign decision on a similarly worded statute binds an Indian court
options.explanation: Foreign decisions are persuasive only, and their weight depends on similarity of language and of social conditions.

options.text: External aids are admissible where the language is ambiguous, and none of them can be used against the plain and unambiguous words of the statute
options.explanation: Correct. This is the governing sentence for the whole topic: aids resolve ambiguity, they do not create it, and the enacted words always prevail.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Literal rule and golden rule
questions.stem: Explain the literal (grammatical) rule of interpretation and the golden rule, bringing out clearly when a court moves from the first to the second and how far it may go when it does. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Literal or grammatical rule: where the words of a statute are plain, clear and unambiguous, they must be given their ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning, whatever the consequence; the letter of the law is the best evidence of its intention, and the court neither adds words nor subtracts them
skeleton.citation: Rule of literal / grammatical construction

skeleton.point: What the rule carries with it: words are read in their ordinary popular sense, or in their technical sense where the statute deals with a particular trade, science or art; a statutory definition governs throughout unless the context otherwise requires; the same word is presumed to bear the same meaning throughout; a casus omissus cannot be supplied by the court; hardship or inconvenience is no ground for departing from clear words
skeleton.citation: Rule of literal construction — casus omissus and the ordinary/technical sense

skeleton.point: Golden rule: the grammatical and ordinary sense of the words is adhered to unless it leads to some absurdity, repugnance or inconsistency with the rest of the instrument, in which case the ordinary sense may be modified so as to avoid that absurdity or inconsistency; the trigger is absurdity or repugnancy, not mere hardship, inconvenience or an unwise result
skeleton.citation: Golden rule of construction

skeleton.point: Limits and the two applications: the departure is permitted only so far as is necessary to remove the absurdity, and no further, so the court does not rewrite the provision into its own preferred rule; narrow application — where a word bears two meanings, the meaning avoiding the absurdity is preferred; wider application — where a word bears only one ordinary meaning, it is modified because the literal result is repugnant to the purpose of the Act
skeleton.citation: Golden rule — extent of departure; narrow and wider applications

questions.topic: Ch 14 · The mischief rule in Heydon's case
questions.stem: State the rule in Heydon's case and explain how a court applies it, including the limits within which it operates. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: When the rule is reached for: where the words of a remedial statute are ambiguous or capable of two readings, and the Act was passed to cure an identified defect in the earlier law; it is the rule of choice for welfare, labour, tenancy, consumer-protection and anti-evasion legislation
skeleton.citation: Mischief rule — occasion for its application

skeleton.point: The four matters to be considered: (i) what was the law before the making of the Act; (ii) what was the mischief and defect for which the prior law did not provide; (iii) what remedy the legislature has resolved and appointed; and (iv) what is the true reason of the remedy
skeleton.citation: Rule in Heydon's case — the four questions

skeleton.point: The court's duty thereafter: to make such construction as will suppress the mischief and advance the remedy, and to suppress subtle inventions and evasions designed to continue the mischief — so that between two available readings the one that leaves the evil in place is rejected
skeleton.citation: Mischief rule — suppress the mischief, advance the remedy

skeleton.point: Limits: the rule does not license the insertion of words, and the chosen reading must still be one the language can bear; it cannot overturn a clear provision; it has little force in penal and taxing statutes, where strict construction governs; and the mischief must be identified from legitimate sources — the prior law, the preamble, the statement of objects and reasons and the historical setting — not from the judge's own view of policy
skeleton.citation: Mischief rule — limits; strict construction of penal and taxing statutes

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis
questions.stem: Explain the maxims noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis, state the conditions for the application of the latter, and indicate the situations in which it does not apply. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Noscitur a sociis — a word is known by the company it keeps: the meaning of a doubtful word is gathered from the words associated with it, associated words being presumed to be used in a related sense and to take colour from one another; it applies to any string of associated words and needs no particular structure. Illustration: in 'place of public resort, dance hall, cinema, theatre or circus', the doubtful expression takes colour from places of entertainment, so a library falls outside
skeleton.citation: Maxim noscitur a sociis

skeleton.point: Ejusdem generis — of the same kind: where general words follow an enumeration of specific words, the general words are confined to things of the same genus as the specific words that precede them; it is a specialised application of noscitur a sociis, not a separate principle
skeleton.citation: Maxim ejusdem generis

skeleton.point: Conditions, all of which must be satisfied: (i) the statute contains an enumeration of specific words; (ii) the subjects of the enumeration constitute a genus or category, having a common characteristic beyond being listed together; (iii) that genus is not exhausted by the enumeration, so the general words have something left to cover; and (iv) the general words follow the specific words, and no contrary legislative intention appears
skeleton.citation: Ejusdem generis — conditions of application

skeleton.point: Where it does not apply: where the specific words form no genus; where the enumeration exhausts the genus, since applying the maxim would make the general words redundant; where a contrary intention appears, as from 'or any other thing whatsoever', 'whether or not of the same kind as the foregoing', or a definition of the general expression; where the general words precede rather than follow the enumeration; and where confining the general words would defeat the object of a remedial provision
skeleton.citation: Ejusdem generis — exclusions; ut res magis valeat quam pereat

questions.stem: What are internal aids to interpretation? Explain the principal internal aids and state the weight each carries. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Meaning: internal aids are guides found inside the statute itself; the statute is read as a whole, and internal aids are resorted to before anything outside it. Governing principle: no aid, however weighty, can be used against the plain and unambiguous words of the statute — aids resolve ambiguity, they do not create it
skeleton.citation: Internal aids — meaning and governing principle

skeleton.point: Long title, short title and preamble: the long title is part of the Act and a legitimate guide to its general scope and object; the short title serves identification only and has no interpretative value; the preamble is part of the Act and is the key to its object and policy, available where the words are ambiguous but never against plain words
skeleton.citation: Internal aids — titles and preamble

skeleton.point: Headings and marginal notes: a heading prefixed to a group of sections may be referred to where the section is ambiguous but cannot control its plain meaning; a marginal or side note is the weakest internal aid, being generally no part of the Act and not inserted by the legislature, and is used only as a rough indication — marginal notes in the Constitution being the recognised exception
skeleton.citation: Internal aids — headings and marginal notes

skeleton.point: Definition or interpretation clause: binding, and the defined meaning governs throughout subject to the words 'unless the context otherwise requires'. The three formulae — 'means' is restrictive and exhaustive; 'includes' is extensive, preserving the ordinary meaning and adding to it, the enumeration being illustrative; 'means and includes' is exhaustive despite the word 'includes'. 'Is deemed to be' creates a legal fiction, carried to its logical conclusion for the stated purpose only
skeleton.citation: Internal aids — definition clauses; means, includes, means and includes, deeming

skeleton.point: Proviso, Explanation and illustrations: a proviso carves an exception out of the provision to which it is attached, operates only on that provision, cannot enlarge it and is not to be read as an independent enactment; an Explanation clarifies and may widen or narrow the main provision but does not stand apart from it; illustrations show how the legislature intended the section to work but cannot modify or extend it, and where an illustration conflicts with the section the section prevails
skeleton.citation: Internal aids — proviso, Explanation and illustrations

skeleton.point: Schedules, non-obstante clauses, punctuation and saving clauses: a Schedule is part of the Act, but on conflict the enacting section prevails; a non-obstante clause ('notwithstanding anything contained in ...') overrides the provisions it displaces to the extent of the inconsistency, while a 'subject to' clause is its mirror and yields; punctuation is of minor value and cannot control the meaning of the words; a saving clause preserves existing rights, pending proceedings or an earlier law and is construed so as not to conflict with the main enactment
skeleton.citation: Internal aids — Schedules, non-obstante and subject-to clauses, punctuation, saving clauses

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by external aids to interpretation, describe the principal external aids, and state the limits within which each may be used. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Meaning and admissibility: external aids lie outside the statute and are resorted to only where the language, read with the internal aids, remains ambiguous; every one of them is subordinate to the words actually enacted
skeleton.citation: External aids — meaning and occasion for use

skeleton.point: Dictionaries, textbooks and historical setting: a dictionary supplies the ordinary meaning of an undefined word, but gives all possible meanings, so the court must select the one that fits the context, and a dictionary can never override a statutory definition or an established trade meaning; textbooks and commentaries are persuasive only; the historical setting — the circumstances, the state of society and the prior law at enactment — establishes the mischief but cannot displace clear words
skeleton.citation: External aids — dictionaries, textbooks, historical setting

skeleton.point: Statement of Objects and Reasons, committee and commission reports, and parliamentary debates: the Statement of Objects and Reasons accompanying a Bill is admissible to understand the background, the mischief and the purpose, but not to construe the section, because the Bill may have been amended in its passage; committee, commission and Law Commission reports are good evidence of the mischief, not of the meaning of the enacted words; parliamentary debates are of limited use — the speech of the mover of the Bill may be looked at for the object and the mischief, but individual members' opinions do not fix the meaning, since what is enacted is the text and not the speeches
skeleton.citation: External aids — Statement of Objects and Reasons, reports, debates

skeleton.point: Other statutes, foreign decisions and usage: statutes in pari materia, that is, dealing with the same subject matter, are read together as one system, though a definition in one Act does not automatically govern another; a later Act may show how the legislature understood the earlier one, and a declaratory or amending Act may settle the question, but a later Act cannot otherwise change the meaning the earlier one bore; foreign decisions on similarly worded statutes are persuasive only, their weight depending on similarity of language and social conditions; long and uniform usage under an old statute is strong evidence of meaning under contemporanea expositio, but is weak for a modern statute; departmental circulars show contemporaneous official understanding but do not bind courts
skeleton.citation: External aids — in pari materia, later statutes, foreign decisions, usage, circulars

skeleton.point: The governing limit, to be stated in terms: aids are admitted to resolve ambiguity and no external aid may be used against the plain and unambiguous words of the statute; the order of operations is therefore fixed — plain words first, then the statute read as a whole with its internal aids, and only then material outside it
skeleton.citation: Interpretation — primacy of the enacted words

questions.stem: Distinguish between mandatory and directory provisions of a statute and explain the tests a court applies to decide into which class a provision falls. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: The distinction and its consequence: a mandatory (imperative) provision must be complied with exactly, and non-compliance invalidates the act done; a directory provision requires only substantial compliance, and non-compliance leaves the act valid, though some other consequence such as a penalty may follow. The question is therefore never 'was the provision broken' but 'does the breach destroy the validity of what was done'
skeleton.citation: Mandatory and directory provisions — the distinction

skeleton.point: 'Shall' and 'may' are not conclusive: 'shall' ordinarily indicates a mandatory provision and 'may' a discretionary one, but the words are used loosely by draftsmen; a 'shall' may be read as directory, and a 'may' as mandatory where a duty is cast or a right is conferred on a person who can demand its exercise. The court decides from the object and scheme of the statute, not from the auxiliary verb
skeleton.citation: Mandatory and directory provisions — 'shall' and 'may'

skeleton.point: The tests: (i) the object of the provision — does the object require exact compliance, or is the provision merely one mode of achieving an object attainable otherwise; (ii) the consequence stated by the statute — a declaration that the act shall be void or of no effect indicates a mandatory provision, whereas the prescription of a penalty alone usually indicates a directory one, the legislature having supplied its own consequence; (iii) prejudice — whether non-compliance causes prejudice or injustice to a person the provision was meant to protect; (iv) serious general inconvenience or injustice to persons who have no control over the default, typically a default by a public officer, which points to a directory reading
skeleton.citation: Mandatory and directory provisions — object, consequence, prejudice and inconvenience tests

skeleton.point: Two further indicators, with illustration: a provision imposing a duty on a public officer for the benefit of the public, with a time limit, is often directory, while a provision conferring a right or safeguard on an individual — notice, hearing, consent — is usually mandatory; and negative or prohibitory language ('no order shall be made unless ...') is a strong indicator of a mandatory provision. Thus a requirement that an officer complete a list by a stated date is directory, while a requirement of fifteen days' notice before an order to a person's prejudice is mandatory
skeleton.citation: Mandatory and directory provisions — public duty, individual safeguard, negative language

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Case: reading a list, and reconciling two sections
questions.case: The (fictitious) Municipal Markets Act 2024 of a model State contains the following provisions. Section 4: 'No person shall sell in a notified market any live poultry, sheep, goats and other livestock except from a licensed pen.' Section 5: 'The Market Committee may regulate the sale of goods in any stall, shed, auction platform or other place of public sale within the market.' Section 18: 'Every trader in a notified market shall pay a licence fee of two thousand rupees a year.' Section 62: 'A trader dealing exclusively in seasonal horticultural produce shall pay a licence fee of five hundred rupees a year.' Devika sells rabbits and ornamental fish from an unlicensed enclosure and deals otherwise only in seasonal fruit. She is prosecuted under section 4 and assessed to a fee of two thousand rupees under section 18.

readLink.label: Read: Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis →

questions.stem: In deciding whether ornamental fish fall within 'other livestock' in section 4, the court should:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ejusdem generis, conditions

options.text: Apply the general words at full width, because 'other livestock' is a general expression and general expressions are read broadly
options.explanation: This ignores the structure of the clause. General words following an enumeration are not read at full width where the enumeration forms a genus.

options.text: Ask whether poultry, sheep and goats form a genus, whether that genus is exhausted, and whether any contrary intention appears — and, finding a genus of farmed food-producing animals that is not exhausted, confine 'other livestock' to that genus, so ornamental fish fall outside
options.explanation: Correct. All four conditions of ejusdem generis are present: an enumeration; a genus (farmed animals kept for food or produce); a genus not exhausted, since cattle, pigs and ducks remain; and general words that follow, with no 'whatsoever' or definition showing a contrary intention. Ornamental fish are not of that genus.

options.text: Apply noscitur a sociis, since general words follow specific words in an enumeration
options.explanation: Noscitur a sociis is the wider parent maxim; where general words follow specific words forming a genus, the specialised application — ejusdem generis — is the correct tool.

options.text: Treat section 4 as void for uncertainty as regards animals not named
options.explanation: Courts construe such provisions; they do not strike them down. Uncertainty about the outer edge of a class is what the maxims exist to resolve.

questions.stem: Suppose section 4 had read 'any live poultry, sheep, goats and other livestock or animals of any description whatsoever'. The effect on the ornamental fish would be:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — ejusdem generis, contrary legislative intention

options.text: No change, since a genus is still present in the first three items
options.explanation: The presence of a genus is only one condition. A manifest contrary intention displaces the maxim even where a genus exists.

options.text: No change, since 'whatsoever' is mere surplusage and surplusage is not to be presumed
options.explanation: The presumption against surplusage cuts the other way: 'whatsoever' must be given work to do, and its work is to widen the general words.

options.text: The fish would be excluded a fortiori, the list having become exhaustive
options.explanation: An expanding formula does not make a list exhaustive; it removes the restriction.

options.text: The fish would be covered: 'animals of any description whatsoever' is a manifest contrary intention which displaces ejusdem generis, and the general words are read at full width
options.explanation: Correct. Expressions such as 'whatsoever' or 'whether or not of the same kind as the foregoing' are standard drafting signals that the legislature intended the general words to be unrestricted.

questions.stem: On the fee, the correct analysis of sections 18 and 62 is:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — harmonious construction and generalia specialibus non derogant

options.text: Section 62, being the special provision, governs a trader dealing exclusively in seasonal horticultural produce, and section 18 governs every other trader; both provisions are thus given effect and neither becomes a dead letter
options.explanation: Correct. Harmonious construction requires that effect be given to both; where they cannot both operate on the same facts, generalia specialibus non derogant makes the special provision govern those facts while the general provision governs the rest. Devika pays five hundred rupees.

options.text: Section 18 prevails because it appears earlier and states the general scheme of the Act
options.explanation: Order of appearance decides nothing, and this reading would leave section 62 with nothing to operate on.

options.text: Both fees are payable, since the Act imposes each in terms
options.explanation: Cumulative application is not the technique of harmonious construction, which confines each provision to its own field rather than stacking them.

options.text: Section 62 must be ignored, since harmony is achieved by applying a single uniform fee
options.explanation: Achieving harmony by ignoring a provision is precisely the subtraction the rule forbids.

questions.stem: In deciding whether a covered handcart parked inside the market is an 'other place of public sale' under section 5, the appropriate maxim is:
questions.sourceRef: Rules of construction — noscitur a sociis

options.text: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius, since handcarts are not mentioned
options.explanation: The maxim of express mention would prove too much: it would exclude everything the general words were inserted to cover.

options.text: Reddendo singula singulis, since the section contains several subjects
options.explanation: There is one subject and a list of places. Nothing needs to be distributed.

options.text: Noscitur a sociis: the doubtful expression takes colour from its companions — stall, shed and auction platform being fixed places of sale within the market — so a movable handcart is doubtful and is likely to fall outside
options.explanation: Correct. The maxim applies to any string of associated words, and here it colours the general expression by reference to the fixed selling places named alongside it.

options.text: Contemporanea expositio, since the Act is recent and the Committee's practice is known
options.explanation: Contemporaneous exposition has little or no application to a modern statute, and the Act here dates from 2024.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Case: a taxing and penal statute construed strictly
questions.case: The (fictitious) Bulk Fuel Cess Act 2024 provides: Section 3 (charge): 'There shall be levied a cess of two per cent on every sale of bulk fuel by a refiner.' Section 9 (exemption): 'No cess shall be payable on a sale to a person holding a certificate of registration as a public transport undertaking.' Section 14 (machinery): 'The assessing authority may, in the prescribed manner, determine and recover the cess.' Section 21 (offence): 'Whoever removes bulk fuel from a refinery without a delivery note shall be punishable with a fine.' Chandan, a fuel blender who is not a refiner, sells bulk fuel and is assessed under section 3. Ishaan, a driver, moves fuel out of a refinery on an oral instruction, unaware that a delivery note was required.

questions.stem: On the assessment of Chandan under section 3, the correct position is:
questions.sourceRef: Strict construction of a charging provision in a taxing statute

options.text: He is liable, because the object of the Act is plainly to tax bulk fuel sales and he is within its spirit
options.explanation: There is no equity about a tax and nothing is to be implied into a charge. Being within the spirit is not enough.

options.text: He is liable, because the mischief rule requires the charge to be read so as to prevent avoidance
options.explanation: The mischief rule has little force in a taxing statute, and it can never be used to bring within the charge a person the words do not catch.

options.text: He is not liable: a charging provision is strictly construed, the charge falls only on a 'refiner', and a person not caught by the letter goes free however plainly he is within the spirit
options.explanation: Correct. The classic position is that in a taxing statute one looks simply at what is clearly said; there is no room for any intendment, nothing to be read in and nothing to be implied.

options.text: He is not liable only if he proves that he did not intend to avoid the cess
options.explanation: Intention is irrelevant to a charge. He escapes because the words do not reach him, not because of his state of mind.

questions.stem: On a claim to the section 9 exemption, which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Strict construction of an exemption; burden on the assessee

options.text: The exemption is construed strictly and the burden of showing that he falls within it lies on the assessee; once he is shown to be within it, the exemption is given full effect
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs are examined regularly: strict construction of exemptions, with the burden on the person claiming, and full effect once the claim is made out.

options.text: The exemption is construed liberally, because exemptions are beneficial provisions
options.explanation: The liberal canon applies to welfare legislation for a protected class, not to fiscal exemptions.

options.text: The burden of disproving the exemption lies on the revenue
options.explanation: The burden of establishing an exemption lies on the person claiming it.

options.text: The exemption cannot apply at all, since a taxing statute admits of no exceptions
options.explanation: A taxing statute contains whatever exceptions the legislature enacts; section 9 is one of them.

questions.stem: How should section 14, the machinery provision, be construed?
questions.sourceRef: Construction of machinery provisions in a taxing statute

options.text: Strictly, like the charging provision, since it forms part of the same fiscal statute
options.explanation: Strict construction of the machinery would frustrate collection of a charge the legislature has validly imposed.

options.text: Strictly, because 'may' confers a discretion which cannot be enlarged
options.explanation: The word 'may' here casts a duty on the assessing authority; and in any event the canon for machinery provisions does not turn on the auxiliary verb.

options.text: It cannot be construed at all until rules are prescribed under it
options.explanation: A provision does not go into abeyance for want of rules; the court construes the section as it stands.

options.text: Liberally, so as to make the charge workable — machinery and procedural provisions for assessment, recovery and appeal are construed so that the charge can be given effect
options.explanation: Correct. Strict construction attaches to the charge and to exemptions; the machinery is construed liberally so that what has been charged can actually be assessed and collected.

questions.stem: On Ishaan's prosecution under section 21, which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Strict construction of penal statutes; presumption of mens rea

options.text: He is guilty, because the section is silent as to intention and silence creates strict liability
options.explanation: Silence points the other way: mens rea is presumed in a penal statute unless expressly excluded or excluded by the clear implication of the scheme.

options.text: The section is construed strictly, mens rea is presumed although the section is silent, and any genuine ambiguity is resolved in favour of the accused — so his ignorance of the requirement is relevant to whether the offence is made out
options.explanation: Correct. Three strands of the penal canon combine: strict construction, the presumption of a guilty mind, and the resolution of ambiguity in the accused's favour.

options.text: He is guilty, because a court may extend the section by analogy to conduct of the same kind
options.explanation: Extension by analogy is exactly what strict construction of a penal provision forbids.

options.text: He is not guilty, because a penal provision in a fiscal statute is always void
options.explanation: No such rule exists. Fiscal statutes routinely and validly create offences.

questions.topic: Ch 14 · Case: internal aids and a compliance failure
questions.case: The (fictitious) Heritage Buildings (Protection) Act 2024 opens with a preamble reciting that it is 'an Act to preserve buildings of historic value from demolition and disfigurement'. Section 12 reads: 'Notwithstanding anything contained in any municipal law for the time being in force, no owner shall demolish a listed building: Provided that an owner may remove a portion certified by an engineer as structurally unsafe. Explanation.— For the purposes of this section, painting over an original facade shall be deemed to be disfigurement.' The marginal note to section 12 reads 'Restriction on demolition'. Section 19 reads: 'No listed building shall be removed from the list unless the owner has been given thirty days' notice and an opportunity of being heard.' The Second Schedule prescribes the form of the notice. Priya paints over the facade of her listed building and also removes an unsafe parapet certified by her engineer; the authority removes another building from the list after seven days' notice.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the words 'Notwithstanding anything contained in any municipal law for the time being in force' in section 12?
questions.sourceRef: Internal aids — non-obstante clause

options.text: Section 12 is subordinate to municipal law, which is more specific to buildings
options.explanation: That is the effect of a 'subject to' clause, which is the mirror image of a non-obstante clause.

options.text: The words are surplusage, since a State Act prevails over municipal law in any event
options.explanation: A non-obstante clause is never treated as surplusage; it is the drafter's chosen device for resolving conflict, and surplusage is not to be presumed.

options.text: Section 12 applies only where municipal law is silent
options.explanation: That again reverses the clause: it applies notwithstanding municipal law, not only in its absence.

options.text: It is a non-obstante clause: section 12 overrides the municipal provisions it displaces, to the extent of the inconsistency
